examples.note: The gustar pattern. History interests me.
Plural subject, plural verb.

examples.en: I'm not interested in that offer.
examples.note: Used for polite refusals.

tricky: '¿Te importa?' with a yes/no answer trips up speakers of English. 'Do you mind?' 'No, no me importa' (I don't mind). Saying 'sí' means you do mind.

title: funcionar vs trabajar
tagline: In English a machine 'works' as well as a person. In Spanish, machines funcionan and people trabajan.

sides.core: To work (of machines, plans, systems) — to function properly.

examples.note: A broken machine. Never 'no trabaja'.

examples.es: Esa idea no va a funcionar.
examples.en: That idea isn't going to work.
examples.note: Plans and ideas can function too.
A common question when learning a gadget.

sides.core: To work as a person — a job, effort, a task.

examples.note: Where you work. Trabajar en + place.
Trabajar de = to work as (a job). 'Trabajar como' also works.
Days off. Also 'trabajo' = work or job.

tricky: 'Mi coche no trabaja' is understood but sounds like the car lacks a job. Always 'funciona'. For people, 'funcionar' is wrong unless you mean something like 'he's not functioning today'.

title: cumplir
tagline: Cumplir means to fulfil — which covers birthdays, promises, rules and sentences. English uses a different verb for each.

sides.core: To turn a given age. The verb for birthdays.

examples.note: Cumplir + age. The number plus 'años' is the object.
Asked about the coming birthday. 'Cuántos años tienes' is how old you are.

examples.es: Mi hija cumplió cinco años ayer.
examples.note: The birthday that just passed.

sides.core: To do what's required — a promise, rule, deadline, sentence.

examples.note: Cumplir una promesa = to keep a promise. 'Mantener' is rarer.

examples.en: You have to follow the rules.
examples.note: Complying with rules and regulations.
Cumplir condena = to serve a sentence.

tricky: 'Cumplir con' is used for duties: 'cumplir con su deber' = to do one's duty. Without 'con' you get a direct object ('cumplió su deber'). Both are fine, but 'con' is more common for abstract obligations.

title: llegar vs alcanzar
tagline: Llegar is arriving. Alcanzar is reaching — by stretching, catching up, or achieving.

sides.core: To arrive at a place or point in time.

examples.note: Arrival time. Llegar a + place.
No preposition needed with 'casa'. Llegar a casa = to arrive home.
Llegar a ser = to end up being. A result after effort.

sides.core: To reach something by stretching, to catch up with, to pass something, or to achieve a goal.

examples.note: Hand something to someone. Very common at the table.
Physical reach.

examples.es: Alcanzaron al ladrón en la esquina.
examples.en: They caught up with the thief at the corner.
examples.note: Catching up. Also 'alcanzar un objetivo' = to reach a goal.

tricky: In Latin America 'alcanzar' also means 'be enough': 'no me alcanza el dinero' = I can't afford it. Same word, new sense.

title: quitar vs quitarse
tagline: Quitar is taking something away. Quitarse is taking off your own clothes or stepping aside. The reflexive points back at you.

sides.core: To remove, take away or clear something.

examples.note: Removing an object from a place.
Taking from someone. The person who loses is the indirect object.
Quitar la mesa = to clear the table. Poner la mesa = to set it.

sides.core: To take off your own clothes or accessories, or to get out of the way.

examples.note: Clothing: the opposite of ponerse.
Body part or clothing comes after the reflexive pronoun.
Idiom, informal. Quitarse de + place.

tricky: 'Quitar los zapatos' means remove someone else's shoes. 'Quitarse los zapatos' is the normal way to take your own off. Don't use 'quitar' for yourself.

title: llevar vs vestirse (wear)
tagline: English 'wear' has no single Spanish match. Llevar is the state of wearing, vestirse is the process of dressing, and ponerse is the act of putting on.

sides.core: To wear — what's on your body right now.

examples.note: Describing someone's usual look.

examples.en: She was wearing a red dress.
examples.note: Imperfect for what someone had on at a moment.
'Puesto' makes it explicit: on you now.

sides.core: To get dressed, or to dress in a style or colour.

examples.en: I get dressed in five minutes.
examples.note: The process. Stem change: visto, vistes.
Vestirse de + colour or role: 'vestirse de payaso'.
Style. Vestirse bien/mal.

tricky: 'Ponerse' = put on, 'llevar' = be wearing, 'vestirse' = get dressed. 'Me pongo el abrigo, llevo el abrigo' — first the action, then the state.

title: ganar vs ganarse
tagline: Ganar is to win or earn. Ganarse is to earn something through your own effort — the reflexive stresses that you've deserved it.

sides.core: To win a contest, earn money or gain something.

examples.note: Winning contests. Also 'ganar un premio'.

examples.en: I earn a thousand euros a month.
examples.note: Salary. Not 'cobrar' for the amount, though cobrar is used for being paid.
Ganar peso = gain weight. Also 'ganar tiempo' = to save time.

sides.core: To earn through effort or deserve — often used with reputation, trust or living.

examples.es: Se ganó la confianza del equipo.
examples.note: Intangible things you win over time.

examples.es: Se gana la vida como fotógrafa.
examples.en: She earns a living as a photographer.
examples.note: Ganarse la vida = to make a living. Fixed phrase.
Deserving something. Also used ironically: 'te lo ganaste a pulso'.

tricky: 'Ganar la vida' sounds like you're winning life. Always 'ganarse la vida'. And 'me ganó' = he beat me; 'me gané' = I earned for myself.

title: soñar
tagline: Soñar con is the key phrase. You dream 'with' something in Spanish, both when sleeping and when aspiring.

sides.core: To dream while asleep. Always soñar con.

examples.en: I dreamed about you last night.
examples.note: Contigo, not 'de ti' or 'sobre ti'.
Soñar con + noun or infinitive.
Nightmares don't use soñar. 'Soñé una pesadilla' is rare.

sides.core: To dream of a future you want, or to daydream.

examples.en: She dreams of becoming an actress.
examples.note: Aspiration. Soñar con + infinitive.
A common saying when someone is fantasising.
Ni soñarlo = no way. Informal refusal.

tricky: Learners say 'soñé de ti' or 'soñé sobre ti' from English 'dream about'. Spanish uses 'con' every time. And 'sueño' is also 'sleepiness': 'tengo sueño' = I'm tired.

title: olvidar vs olvidarse
tagline: Olvidar is to forget something. Olvidarse de is the same thing in a more personal way — and 'se me olvidó' is the structure that makes it accidental.

sides.core: To forget — direct object, you as the subject.

examples.note: A simple statement. You are the one who forgot.
Emotional memory. Also 'olvidar' = to put out of mind.
Let it go. A common answer to 'never mind'.

sides.core: To forget — reflexive, with olvidarse de, or the accidental 'se me olvidó'.

examples.note: Olvidarse de + thing. You are still the subject.
'Se me olvidó' puts the forgotten thing as the subject. It happened to me, it wasn't my fault.
The verb agrees with the forgotten item (billetes → olvidaron).

tricky: 'Olvidé las llaves' (I left the keys behind) can mean physically leaving them somewhere. 'Se me olvidaron las llaves' is the softer, no-blame option.

title: notar vs fijarse
tagline: Notar is to notice or sense passively. Fijarse is to pay attention on purpose — to look carefully.

sides.core: To notice, to sense, to feel that something is the case.

examples.note: Perception without effort.
Se nota = it's obvious, it shows. Very common.
Not perceiving something.

sides.core: To pay attention, to look closely, to notice on purpose — fijarse en.

examples.note: Directing attention. Fijarse en + thing.
Asking if someone paid attention.

examples.en: Just imagine! / Would you believe it!
examples.note: Idiomatic reaction to surprising news.

tricky: 'Noté su corbata' is just a passing observation. 'Me fijé en su corbata' means you paid attention to it, perhaps because it was odd or striking.

title: preocupar vs preocuparse
tagline: Preocupar means 'to worry someone' — gustar-style. Preocuparse means 'to worry yourself'. Both are common and easy to mix up.

sides.core: To worry, concern someone — the cause is the subject.

examples.note: The cause is the subject. Gustar pattern.
Asking what's on someone's mind.
Negative: not a source of concern.

sides.core: To worry, to take care or be concerned about someone — you are the subject.

examples.note: The most common use. Command to relax.
Preocuparse por/de + person or thing.
General trait.

tricky: 'Estoy preocupado' (I'm worried) is the state. 'Me preocupo' is the habit or the act. And 'preocuparse de' can mean 'to take care of': 'yo me preocupo de la cena' = I'll see to dinner.

title: resultar
tagline: Resultar means 'to turn out' — but also fills gaps where Spanish avoids ser or tener, especially with 'me resulta'.

sides.core: To turn out, to prove to be, or to end up.

examples.en: The film turned out to be boring.
examples.note: Unexpected evaluation after the fact.

examples.en: It turns out that he had no money.
examples.note: Resulta que = it turns out that. A great narrative opener.

examples.es: El plan resultó ser un desastre.
examples.en: The plan turned out to be a disaster.
examples.note: Resultar ser + noun.

sides.core: To be or seem, with an indirect object — it 'resultas' something to you.

examples.en: I find it hard to understand.
examples.note: Me resulta + adjective = I find it. Smoother than 'es difícil para mí'.

examples.en: It's strange to see you here.
examples.note: Personal reaction to a situation.
News language: resultar herido = to be injured.

tricky: 'Resultar' is often a more elegant way to say 'ser' or 'encontrar': 'me resulta imposible' = I find it impossible. Don't confuse it with 'resultado' (the noun) in other places.

title: sobrar vs bastar
tagline: Sobrar means there's too much or some left over. Bastar means that's enough. Neighbours on the same scale.

sides.core: To be left over or to be more than needed — works like gustar.

examples.note: Leftovers. Also 'las sobras' = leftovers.

examples.en: I have two euros to spare.
examples.note: What's left after paying. Gustar pattern.
Strong idiom: you're superfluous.

sides.core: To be enough, to suffice.

examples.note: Short and idiomatic. Basta con + noun.

examples.en: All you have to do is let me know.
examples.note: Basta con que + subjunctive.
A firm demand to stop. Used by parents and teachers.

tricky: 'Bastante' (quite, enough) is an adverb from bastar. 'Hay bastante comida' = there's enough food; 'sobra comida' = there's more than enough.

title: costar vs valer
tagline: Both express price. Costar is what you pay. Valer is what something is worth. Valer also means 'to be okay'.

sides.core: To cost — and to be difficult or take effort.

examples.en: How much does this coat cost?
examples.note: The standard price question.

examples.en: It cost me a lot of effort.
examples.note: Costar for effort, not just money.

examples.en: I find it hard to get up early.
examples.note: Costar + infinitive = to find it difficult.

sides.core: To be worth, to be valid, to be acceptable.

examples.en: How much is this house worth?
examples.note: Valuation, often large amounts.
Valer la pena = to be worth it. Fixed phrase.
The single most common word in Spain for agreeing. Literally 'it's valid'.

tricky: 'Cuesta' and 'vale' overlap for prices, but 'cuánto cuesta' is the shop question. 'Cuánto vale' feels more appraisal-like. And 'valer' in Latin America is less used for 'okay', where 'ok' or 'dale' appear.

title: durar vs tardar
tagline: Both measure time. Durar is how long something lasts. Tardar is how long it takes to get done or arrive.

sides.core: To last — how long something continues.

examples.note: The event has a length.

examples.es: Esta batería dura todo el día.
examples.note: Lifespan of an object.
General truth.

sides.core: To take time, to be late — the time needed for a person or process to complete something.

examples.en: It takes me twenty minutes to get there.
examples.note: Tardar + time + en + infinitive.
Asked while someone gets ready or is on the way.
A common send-off. Also 'tarde' = late.

tricky: 'El viaje dura tres horas' (the journey lasts three hours) vs 'tardo tres horas en llegar' (it takes me three hours to arrive). The first describes the thing, the second the person.

title: pagar vs cobrar
tagline: Pagar is handing over money. Cobrar is receiving it — as a wage, a fee or a bill.

sides.core: To pay, to hand money over — for something, to someone.

examples.note: Offering to cover the bill.
Pagar con tarjeta/efectivo. No direct object needed.
A medias = half each.

sides.core: To charge, to collect payment, to earn a wage.

examples.en: I get paid at the end of the month.
examples.note: Receiving a salary. The employee is the subject.
The shop or bank is the one charging.
Said to a waiter. Literally 'can you charge me?'. Also 'la cuenta, por favor' works.

tricky: 'Cobrar' has both directions: you charge a client or you collect your salary. 'Cobrar vida' means to come to life. 'Pagar' is always the one handing money over.

title: mandar vs enviar
tagline: Both mean 'to send'. Enviar is neutral and a touch formal; mandar is common in speech and also means 'to order'.

sides.core: To send — letters, emails, packages, people.

examples.es: Te envío el archivo por correo.
examples.en: I'm sending you the file by email.
examples.note: Slightly formal. Common in writing.

examples.es: Enviaron un paquete a mi casa.
examples.en: They sent a package to my house.
examples.note: Postal and delivery contexts.

examples.es: Han enviado a un enviado especial.
examples.en: They have sent a special envoy.
examples.note: Sending a person on a mission. Enviado = envoy.

sides.core: To send in everyday speech, and to order or be in charge.

examples.note: Casual, spoken. Very common in Latin America.

examples.es: Mandó a su hijo a la tienda.
examples.en: She sent her son to the shop.
examples.note: Mandar a + person + a + place.

examples.en: My mum is the boss here.
examples.note: Mandar = to be in command. '¿Mande?' in Mexico = pardon?

tricky: 'Mandar a alguien a paseo' / 'mandar a freír espárragos' = to tell someone to get lost. Mandar covers more idioms than enviar.

title: casarse
tagline: Casarse con — you marry 'with' someone in Spanish. The preposition and the reflexive are both non-negotiable.

sides.core: To get married. Always reflexive and always followed by con.

examples.es: Se casó con su mejor amigo.
examples.note: Casarse con + person. Never 'casó a'.
Plural for the couple. Reflexive pronoun nos.
Vosotros form, used in Spain.

sides.core: Estar casado is the state; casar is to marry someone off (an officiant).

examples.note: The state of being married. Estar casado/a. Not 'ser casado'.
The officiant does the marrying. No reflexive.
Recién casados. Also 'los novios' = bride and groom.

tricky: 'Me casé a ella' is a classic mistake. Use 'me casé con ella'. Also 'me divorcié de' (not 'con').

title: despedir vs despedirse
tagline: Despedir is to fire someone or see them off. Despedirse is to say goodbye yourself.

sides.core: To fire an employee, to see someone off, or to give off (smell, light).

examples.en: They fired him for being late.
examples.note: The standard word for dismissal. 'Echar' is a colloquial alternative.

examples.en: We went to see her off at the airport.
examples.note: Saying goodbye as someone leaves.
Emitting something. Stem change like pedir: despido, despides.

sides.core: To say goodbye — despedirse de.

examples.note: Always despedirse de + person.
A parent's command to a child.

examples.en: She said goodbye with a kiss.
examples.note: How you say goodbye: con + noun.

tricky: 'Me despidieron' = I was fired. 'Me despedí' = I said goodbye. Learners often say 'me despedí' for 'I was laid off' and cause a puzzled look.

title: morir vs matar
tagline: Morir is to die. Matar is to kill. The reflexive forms morirse and matarse change the tone completely.

sides.core: To die. Morirse is more colloquial and used for figurative death.

examples.note: Formal and written. Stem change o→ue: muero, mueres.
Morirse is the usual word in speech for a death in the family.
Figurative: morirse de hambre/risa/frío/sueño.

sides.core: To kill, or to kill oneself accidentally or figuratively.

examples.note: Deliberate killing.

examples.en: He was killed in an accident.
examples.note: Matarse = to die by accident, or to kill oneself, context decides.
Figurative. Also 'matar el tiempo' = to kill time.

tricky: 'Está muerto' = he's dead (state). 'Lo mataron' = they killed him. 'Murió' alone doesn't say anyone caused it. In news, 'murió' vs 'fue asesinado' matters.

title: oler vs saber a
tagline: Oler is smell and saber a is taste — but saber is also 'to know'. The preposition 'a' signals flavour.

sides.core: To smell — both to give off a smell and to perceive one. Oler a = to smell of.

examples.note: Irregular: huelo, hueles. Add h before ue.
Oler a + noun = to smell like.
Question form. Note a qué.

sides.core: To taste of — flavour. Not 'probar', which means to try.

examples.note: Saber a + flavour.
Same pattern as oler: a qué.
Saber + adjective for quality of taste.

tricky: 'Sé a fresa' would be 'I know of strawberry' — nonsense. For taste use the third person: 'sabe a'. And 'huelo' (I smell) vs 'huele' (it smells) is a different thing from 'sabe' vs 'sé'.

title: cerrar vs apagar
tagline: English 'turn off' has two Spanish forms. Cerrar closes taps, doors, accounts. Apagar switches off lights, devices, flames.

sides.core: To close or shut — doors, windows, taps, shops.

examples.note: Stem change e→ie: cierro, cierras.
Taps and gas are closed, not apagados.
Shop opening hours.

sides.core: To switch off electrical devices, lights, flames.

examples.note: The opposite of encender.

examples.es: Apaga el móvil en el cine.
examples.en: Switch your phone off in the cinema.
examples.note: Devices. 'Apagar el ordenador' too.

examples.en: The firefighters put out the fire.
examples.note: Flames and cigarettes: apagar.

tricky: 'Cerrar la luz' is a common Latin American usage in some regions, but in Spain it sounds odd. And 'apagar el grifo' doesn't exist — taps are closed, not switched off.

title: arreglar vs arreglarse
tagline: Arreglar is fixing, tidying or sorting something. Arreglarse is getting ready and managing — the reflexive brings it back to you.

sides.core: To repair, tidy up, sort out or alter.

examples.es: Arregló el coche en un día.
examples.en: He fixed the car in a day.
examples.note: Repairing. 'Reparar' also works but is more formal.
Tidying. Also 'ordenar'.

examples.en: I'll sort it out with her.
examples.note: Resolving a problem between people.

sides.core: To get ready, dress up, manage, or work out.

examples.en: I'm getting ready to go out.
examples.note: Dressing up, doing hair and makeup.
Arreglárselas = to cope, to get by. Fixed phrase.
Se impersonal: things work out.

tricky: 'Arreglarse el pelo' (do your hair) vs 'arreglar el pelo a alguien' (do someone's hair). The reflexive tells you whose hair it is.

title: pegar
tagline: Pegar means to hit, to stick and to match — three unrelated meanings, plus a family of 'give a shout/jump' expressions.

sides.core: To hit someone or to glue/stick something.

examples.note: Hitting. Pegar a + person.

examples.es: Pega la foto en el álbum.
examples.en: Stick the photo in the album.
examples.note: Gluing. The noun is 'pegamento' = glue.

examples.es: Se me ha pegado el arroz.
examples.en: The rice has stuck to the pan.
examples.note: Pegarse = to stick, to burn on the pan, or to catch (a habit).

sides.core: To go with or suit, and to deliver a physical action: a shout, a jump, a fright.

examples.es: Esa camisa no pega con los pantalones.
examples.en: That shirt doesn't go with the trousers.
examples.note: Pegar con = to match. Informal.
Pegar un grito/salto/susto/portazo = to shout, jump, frighten, slam.
Figurative: a trend or season arriving strongly.

tricky: 'Me he pegado con la puerta' = I bumped into the door. Whether pegar means 'hit' or 'stick' depends on context, and the reflexive adds a third reading: to catch something (pegarse un resfriado).

title: meter vs poner
tagline: Poner places something on a surface. Meter puts something inside. 'Put' needs two verbs in Spanish.

sides.core: To put inside — into a container, a space, a situation.

examples.es: Mete la ropa en la maleta.
examples.en: Put the clothes in the suitcase.
examples.note: Into a container. The preposition 'en' marks the place.
Meterse = to get into. Also 'meterse en problemas'.

examples.en: Don't get involved in my business!
examples.note: Meterse en = to interfere. Also 'meter la pata' = to put your foot in it.

sides.core: To put on a surface, to place or position something.

examples.es: Pon el libro sobre la mesa.
examples.en: Put the book on the table.
examples.note: On a surface. Preposition 'sobre' or 'en'.
General placing. The position is open.

examples.en: Where have you put your glasses?
examples.note: Irregular past participle: puesto.

tricky: Both can translate 'put', so check the destination. Is it inside something? Use meter. On top of something? Poner. 'Pon la llave en la cerradura' is fine, but 'mete la llave' stresses the insertion.

title: andar vs caminar
tagline: Both mean 'to walk'. Caminar is the neutral verb. Andar is looser and often means 'to be' or 'to go about'.

sides.core: To walk — the physical action, often a purposeful journey on foot.

examples.es: Camino al trabajo todos los días.
examples.en: I walk to work every day.
examples.note: Standard walking.
As a noun-like subject.
Journey or exploration on foot.

sides.core: To walk, to go about, to be (in a state), and to work (of a device).

examples.es: Anda por la calle sin mirar.
examples.en: He walks down the street without looking.
examples.note: Casual walking.

examples.en: He's looking for a job (these days).
examples.note: Andar + gerund = to be doing something over a period.
Exclamation of disbelief. Also 'anda' for surprise or encouragement.

tricky: '¿Cómo andas?' = how are you getting on? 'No anda' for a machine means it's not working (common in Argentina). Andar covers many moods; caminar is always on foot.

title: comprender vs entender
tagline: Both mean 'to understand'. Entender is the everyday verb. Comprender suggests deeper or empathetic understanding — and also means 'to include'.

sides.core: To understand — language, instructions, how something works.

examples.note: Stem change e→ie: entiendo.
Checking that you're clear.
Entender de = to be knowledgeable about.

sides.core: To understand fully, to empathise — or to comprise.

examples.note: Empathy. 'Te entiendo' can sound more practical.

examples.es: No comprendo por qué lo hizo.
examples.en: I don't understand why he did it.
examples.note: Motives and feelings.
Comprender also means to include, to consist of.

tricky: 'Comprar' (buy) and 'comprender' (understand) differ by two letters but are not related. 'Entender' is also used for opinions: 'a mi entender' = in my understanding.

title: discutir vs comentar
tagline: 'Discuss' is a false friend. Discutir means to argue. Comentar is to talk through, remark on or mention.

sides.core: To argue, quarrel — a heated exchange.

examples.note: A row. Discutir por + reason.

examples.en: I don't want to argue with you.
examples.note: A common phrase to avoid conflict.
A couple or family quarrel.

sides.core: To discuss, comment on, mention, talk over casually.

examples.note: Conversational. 'Te comento' = I'll fill you in.

examples.en: We talked about the film on the way out.
examples.note: Casual discussion of an experience.
Comentar = to remark. 'Comentario' = comment.

tricky: 'Vamos a discutir el contrato' sounds like you plan to fight over it. For a neutral talk, use 'hablar de' or 'tratar'. In formal Latin American contexts, 'discutir' can be neutral — region matters.

title: tratar vs tratarse
tagline: Tratar de is to try. Tratar a is to treat someone. Tratarse de is 'it's about'. Three prepositions, three meanings.

sides.core: To try (tratar de), to treat or behave towards (tratar a), to deal with (tratar sobre).

examples.en: I try to arrive on time.
examples.note: Tratar de + infinitive. Same as intentar.
Behaviour towards someone. Tratar a + person.

examples.es: El libro trata sobre la guerra.
examples.note: Subject matter. Tratar de/sobre.

sides.core: To be about, to concern — an impersonal use, always with 'se' and 'de'.

examples.note: The standard question for a plot or a meeting.
Se trata de + noun = it's a matter of.
Se trata de + infinitive = the point is to.

tricky: 'Tratar' with a subject like 'la película' = the film is about. But 'se trata de' has no real subject. 'La película se trata de amor' is a heard error — say 'la película trata de amor'.

title: dedicar vs dedicarse
tagline: Dedicar is to devote or dedicate something. Dedicarse a is to do for a living — the question '¿a qué te dedicas?' is everywhere.

sides.core: To devote time, effort or a work to someone or something.

examples.es: Dedico dos horas al día a estudiar.
examples.en: I spend two hours a day studying.
examples.note: Devoting time. Dedicar + time + a.

examples.en: He dedicated a song to her.
examples.note: A tribute.

examples.es: Dedica mucho tiempo a su familia.
examples.en: He devotes a lot of time to his family.
examples.note: Priority.

sides.core: To work as, to be occupied with — dedicarse a + noun or infinitive.

examples.en: What do you do for a living?
examples.note: The standard question about someone's job. Not '¿qué haces?' alone.
Dedicarse a + noun.

examples.en: He sells cars for a living.
examples.note: Dedicarse a + infinitive.

tricky: '¿A qué te dedicas?' needs 'a'. Saying '¿qué te dedicas?' is a common mistake. And 'me dedico a' answers it: 'me dedico a la informática'.

title: hay que vs tener que
tagline: Both express obligation. Hay que is impersonal — 'one has to'. Tener que is personal and names who must do it.

sides.core: Impersonal necessity — a general rule for everyone, no subject. Only the 'hay' form is used in the present.

examples.en: We have to wait. / One has to wait.
examples.note: No subject. A general or shared necessity.
No hay que = there's no need to. Not 'it's forbidden'.
Future: habrá que. Past: había que.

sides.core: Personal obligation — a specific person must do something.

examples.note: The subject is 'I'. Conjugates.
Personal recommendation.

examples.en: We had to wait two hours.
examples.note: Preterite tuvimos. Obligation completed in the past.

tricky: 'No tienes que ir' = you don't have to go (it's optional). 'No hay que ir' = one shouldn't go / there's no need. Spanish negation of obligation can mean 'don't have to' or 'must not' depending on the verb, so check the context.

title: aprobar vs suspender
tagline: English 'pass' an exam is aprobar, not pasar. And suspender is to fail — but also to suspend and cancel.

sides.core: To pass an exam, approve a proposal, or give approval.

examples.note: Aprobar = to pass. Stem change o→ue: apruebo.
Passing a law or proposal.

examples.en: I don't approve of his behaviour.
examples.note: Moral approval.

sides.core: To fail an exam (Spain), to suspend, to call off.

examples.note: In Spain, suspender = to fail. In Latin America 'reprobar' or 'perder'.

examples.es: Suspendieron el concierto por la lluvia.
examples.en: They called off the concert because of rain.
examples.note: Cancel.
Disciplinary suspension.

tricky: 'Pasar un examen' means to take an exam in some regions, so 'pasé el examen' can be ambiguous. Use 'aprobé' for passing and 'suspendí' (or 'reprobé' in Latin America) for failing.

title: caber
tagline: Caber means 'to fit inside'. It's irregular, little-used by learners, and has several idioms with a surprising reach.

sides.core: To fit inside something — physical or abstract space.

examples.en: There's no more room for people.
examples.note: Irregular: quepo, cabes, cabe. Present only.

examples.en: Can we all fit in the car?
examples.note: A natural question. Caber en = to fit in.

examples.es: Esta mesa no cabe por la puerta.
examples.en: This table won't fit through the door.
examples.note: Por for movement through.

sides.core: Abstract use: possible, appropriate, or conceivable.

examples.note: A frequent expression. No cabe duda de que + indicative.

examples.es: No me cabe en la cabeza.
examples.en: I can't get my head around it.
examples.note: Used for things you can't accept or understand.
Formal writing. Cabe + infinitive = it's possible or fitting to.

tricky: 'Quepo' (I fit) is one of the strangest first-person forms in Spanish, and subjunctive is 'quepa'. Nobody expects learners to master it, but 'no cabe duda' is worth memorising.

title: disfrutar vs gozar
tagline: Both mean 'to enjoy'. Disfrutar is the everyday word. Gozar is more formal and often means to possess a benefit, like good health.

sides.core: To enjoy — an experience, an activity, a moment. Usually disfrutar de, or no preposition for activities.

examples.note: Disfrutar de + noun. The 'de' is standard but often dropped.
Disfrutar + gerund.
A common send-off. Subjunctive of wish.

sides.core: To enjoy in a deeper or formal sense — to have a benefit or privilege. Gozar de.

examples.note: Possession of a good thing. 'Enjoy' as 'have', not 'have fun'.
Formal language about rights or benefits.

examples.en: They took great pleasure in the music.
examples.note: Strong enjoyment. In some regions it can carry sexual overtones, so avoid in casual speech.

tricky: 'Gozar' is rarely the safe choice for casual enjoyment. 'Disfrutar' fits every situation: 'disfruta de las vacaciones'. Reserve 'gozar de' for good health, rights, reputation.
